issue.title: A think tank says rules and taxes make up to 57% of a new flat's price
issue.question: Some rules and taxes on new homes may be pushing prices up. Which should be cut to build more: affordable housing duties, green and design standards, or taxes like stamp duty?
issue.summary: The Centre for Policy Studies, a think tank, published a report called Easing the Burdens, covered on 10 November 2026. It models two developments and claims government-imposed costs are 57% of the minimum viable price of an inner London flat and 42% of a Home Counties house. The costs it counts include affordable housing duties, stamp duty, the Community Infrastructure Levy, Biodiversity Net Gain and building specifications. The conclusions rest on two modelled developments, not a full assessment of new-build homes. Separate research reported on 9 November found 69% of those asked blamed resource shortages in local planning authorities for delays.

bench.title: Keep the rules and taxes; fund planning teams, refund late decisions
bench.answer: Keep today's rules and taxes, and fix the referee. The housing department ring-fences planning fees and adds funding so each local planning authority can staff its planning team. If a standard housing application is decided late, the authority refunds the fee. The case: the 57% figure comes from two modelled developments, not a full assessment of new homes (s1), so cutting standards or affordable housing duties on it is a gamble. Separate research found 69% of respondents cited resource shortages in planning authorities as a cause of delay (s2). How we'd know: each authority publishes its share of decisions made on time, median wait, and homes started on approved sites, every quarter.

bench.title: Let a national planning service take over stalled housing decisions
bench.answer: Government sets up a national planning service of qualified planners. Any council short of staff can hand it housing applications, and it must decide within a fixed deadline. Councils keep the final say on design. Fees on applications are ring-fenced to pay for it. Leave stamp duty, affordable-housing duties and green standards alone for now: the think tank's 57% figure rests on two modelled developments, not a full assessment (s1), while 69% of respondents in separate research blamed resource shortages in local planning authorities for delays (s2). You'd know it worked if the time from application to decision falls, councils report fewer staffing delays, and affordable homes on big sites don't drop.

bench.title: Cut stamp duty for homes steered by their residents
bench.answer: In this simulation, Parliament should offer stamp duty relief on land bought by resident-owned housing groups. Future residents would elect the board and hire builders through open bids. Relief would depend on published accounts, a completion deadline and resale rules that keep the saving in the homes. Miss those terms and repay the relief. Keep affordable housing duties, safety, quality and green standards. The report models only two developments; that is too narrow a basis for sweeping cuts (s1). Councils should track completion times, prices against local wages and defects. Expand the scheme only if homes arrive sooner, cost less and meet those standards.

gate.verdict: All three answers pass every limit the citizens set, and none eases rules for small builders. Whether cutting taxes, speeding planning or changing who builds does most for ordinary-wage homes cannot be settled by these sources.

jury.question: To get more homes ordinary-wage people can afford, should government first fund planning, cut a tax, or back resident-run building?
options: Fund planning staff and set decision deadlines
Cut taxes like stamp duty on new homes
Back resident-run housing with tax relief
jury.ruling: Tied 5 to 5 between funding planning and cutting taxes; by the tie rule the ruling goes to funding planning staff with decision deadlines, the option the gate found safest.

minister.trial: In three councils that volunteer, a small team of qualified planners decides standard housing applications within a fixed deadline, and the council refunds the fee if it is late. Quarterly, each publishes decisions on time, median wait and homes started on approved sites.
minister.fail_number: Fewer than 80% of standard housing applications decided on time at the end of the trial, or any fall in affordable homes agreed on big sites.
minister.statement: Five jurors said cut the tax. Five said fund planning. A tie, so the safer one goes first. One report, two modelled sites, is no reason to rip up safety or affordable homes. A council with no planners cannot approve a shed. So: three councils, a deadline, fee back if they miss it. Count the roofs. A promise is not a wall.
